      All definitions
      Tier Zero
      The accounts, groups and servers that control the whole domain: domain controllers, Domain Admins and similar groups, the AD CS servers, and the GPOs and containers above them. Whoever controls one of them controls everything.
      Status
      Critical: a group that holds nearly every account (Domain Users, Authenticated Users, Everyone) can reach Tier Zero, or a critical finding is open. High: at least one account outside Tier Zero can reach it. Moderate: no account can, but findings at medium or above are open. Low: no account can, and nothing at medium or above is open. Any path into Tier Zero is a way to take over the domain, so the status is never Low while one is open, however small a share of the domain it is. The line under it says why, as what an attacker can do.
      Accounts with an attack path to Tier Zero
      Enabled users and computers outside Tier Zero with a full path to it. Each is a way in: an attacker who takes over any one of them can take over the domain.
      Share of active accounts
      The same accounts as a share of the active users and computers (enabled, outside Tier Zero, logged on in the last 90 days before the collection). It doesn't set the status.
      Plan steps
      The fewest changes that cut every attack path to Tier Zero, the one that cuts the most first. Weak accounts and hygiene findings need their own fix.
      Open findings
      Findings not fixed or accepted as a risk. Attack path findings are on a path to Tier Zero and are rated by how many users and computers can use them; hygiene findings are weaknesses not on an attack path.
      Tier Zero protected
      The share of Tier Zero objects that no open attack path finding leads to. A Privilege Zone has its own.
      Collection
      The share of active computers whose sessions and local groups were collected. Paths through logged-on sessions and local administrator rights are only as complete as these numbers; below 80% for a domain, the counts can read low. Not targeted means the collector was not asked to read them. A Quick collection reads the directory only, so its counts are compared only with runs that also didn't read them.
      Tiers
      Tier Zero and each Privilege Zone in the settings: its status, the accounts outside it (and outside Tier Zero) with an attack path to it, and how many of its objects are protected. With a run history, a status that changed says what it was the run before. The remediation path is worked out for Tier Zero only; a zone shows its count.
      Since the last run
      The change from the previous run of the same environment in the run history, when there is one; "What changed" lists it line by line. Besides the counts, it names what they don't show: older findings that gained or lost objects, new members of Tier Zero and the zones, and paths into them that appeared or went. Counts measured another way (an older exposure basis) are not compared. A run is compared with the last run that targeted the same sessions and local groups; when there is none, with the run just before, and then it says its counts are not compared.
      Introduced
      Net new over a period: a finding first seen in it (New), a finding fixed before and back in it (Back), an older finding that gained objects in it (+N objects), a new member of Tier Zero or a zone, or a new path into one. The Findings tab filters by it.
      First seen
      When Pathwarden first found a finding, an object in it, a member or a path: the date of that run ("first seen Oct 18 (run 3)"), not when the change was made in the directory. Objects, members and paths are dated from the first run that began dating them; one that left and returned is "back".
      New paths and members
      A new member: an object that joined Tier Zero or a Privilege Zone, such as a user added to Domain Admins. A new path: a relationship into Tier Zero or a zone from outside it (a permission, an admin right, a session) that wasn't there at the run before. A zone with more than 50,000 of either is counted, not dated.

                CriticalPW-006Kerberoastable account with Tier Zero access10 findings
                How to fix this kind of findingstep-by-step guide

                Category: Attack path Typical owner: AD / identity team with the service owner

                What this finding means

                A user account with a service principal name (SPN) is in Tier Zero or has a path to it. Any domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket for it, and that ticket is encrypted with a key derived from the account's password.

                Group and standalone managed service accounts (gMSA, sMSA) are not reported: the domain gives them a 240-byte (120-character) random password and rotates it, so their tickets can't be cracked. In SharpHound collections Pathwarden recognizes them from the gmsa and msa flags; in RustHound-CE and built-in collections, which have no such flag, from the computer-account bit (userAccountControl 0x1000) on a user object. In those collections a user account an administrator gave the computer-account bit by hand, which still has a human-set password, is treated as managed and not reported: check SPN accounts with that bit (Get-ADUser -LDAPFilter "(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4096)") if you collect with RustHound-CE or the built-in collector.

                Why attackers care

                Kerberoasting (Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting, T1558.003) needs only a normal domain account: request tickets for every SPN, take them offline and crack the passwords. Service account passwords are often old, human-chosen and never rotated, and RC4 tickets crack quickly. A cracked privileged service account means domain compromise without any alert on the target.

                Before you change anything

                • Identify the service using the SPN (setspn -L <Account>), the computers running it, and who owns it.
                • Check whether the SPN is still used: event 4769 on domain controllers shows service ticket requests for the account. No requests over weeks often means a stale SPN.
                • If the account is privileged only because of a group it does not need (common for old SQL service accounts in Domain Admins), removing that membership is part of the fix.

                Fix

                Option A: Move the service to a group Managed Service Account (recommended)
                1. Create a gMSA (New-ADServiceAccount) allowed for the service's computers.
                2. Install it on the computers (Install-ADServiceAccount) and change the service to run as <Domain>\<gMSA>$ with an empty password.
                3. Move the SPNs to the gMSA, then disable the old account. gMSA passwords are 240-byte (120-character) random values rotated automatically: not crackable.
                Option B: Remove unneeded SPNs or privileges

                Remove stale SPNs with setspn -D, and remove the account from privileged groups it does not need.

                Option C: If the account must stay

                Set a random password of 25+ characters, enable AES-only Kerberos for the account ("This account supports Kerberos AES 128/256 bit encryption" in ADUC Account tab), then change the password once more so the account has AES keys: a password set before the domain supported AES has none, and with AES only the service stops working. Rotate the password on a schedule after that.

                PowerShell
                Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Kerberoastable user accounts
Get-ADUser -Filter { ServicePrincipalName -like "*" } -Properties ServicePrincipalName, PasswordLastSet, MemberOf

# Option A: create a gMSA (needs a KDS root key in the forest)
New-ADServiceAccount -Name "<gMSA>" -DNSHostName "<gMSA>.<Domain>" `
    -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword "<ServerGroup>"
Install-ADServiceAccount -Identity "<gMSA>"     # run on each service computer

# Option B: remove a stale SPN
setspn -D <SPN> <Account>

# Option C: AES only (0x18 = AES128 + AES256), then reset the password
Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Replace @{ 'msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes' = 24 }
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity "<Account>" -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString "New password")

                Verify

                Get-ADUser "<Account>" -Properties ServicePrincipalName shows no SPNs (Options A/B), or msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes is 24 and PasswordLastSet is recent (Option C). Collect again (or use Retest on the finding) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

                Rollback

                Re-register an SPN with setspn -S <SPN> <Account>; switch the service back to the old account in the Services console. Keep the old account disabled, not deleted, until the gMSA has run cleanly for a while.

                References

                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/
                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/group-managed-service-accounts/group-managed-service-accounts-overview

                CriticalPW-007Kerberos pre-authentication disabled (AS-REP roasting)5 findings
                How to fix this kind of findingstep-by-step guide

                Category: Attack path or hygiene (hygiene when the account has no path to Tier Zero) Typical owner: AD / identity team

                What this finding means

                The account has "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" set. Anyone who can reach a domain controller can request an authentication response for it without knowing its password, and part of that response is encrypted with the password.

                Why attackers care

                AS-REP roasting (Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting, T1558.004) does not even need a domain account: an attacker on the network asks for the response and cracks it offline. If the password is weak, they get the account; if the account is privileged or has a path to Tier Zero, that is domain compromise.

                Before you change anything

                • The flag is almost always a leftover from old Unix/Kerberos interop or a vendor install guide. Ask the account owner which system uses it.
                • Check recent use: event 4768 on domain controllers with "Pre-Authentication Type" 0 for this account shows clients authenticating without pre-auth.
                • Very old MIT Kerberos or Java clients may fail once pre-auth is required; test with the owning application.

                Fix

                Option A: Require pre-authentication (recommended)
                1. Active Directory Users and Computers > the account > Properties > Account.
                2. Under Account options, clear Do not require Kerberos preauthentication.
                3. OK, then test the application that uses the account.
                Option B: If an application genuinely needs it

                Keep the flag only with a long random password (25+ characters), no privileged group memberships, and monitoring of event 4768 for that account.

                PowerShell
                Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# All accounts with pre-authentication disabled
Get-ADUser -Filter { DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true } -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth, Enabled

# Require pre-authentication again
Set-ADAccountControl -Identity "<Account>" -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false

# Option B: set a long random password if the flag must stay
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity "<Account>" -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString "New password")

                Verify

                Get-ADUser "<Account>" -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth must show False. Collect again (or use Retest on the finding) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

                Rollback

                Set-ADAccountControl -Identity "<Account>" -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $true restores the previous behavior if an application breaks; then plan Option B for that account.

                References

                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/004/
                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/activedirectory/set-adaccountcontrol

                Clear the account option 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' (the userAccountControl flag DONT_REQ_PREAUTH) on SVC-00003@SCALE.LOCAL. If an application needs it, give the account a random password of 25 or more characters. If the account is no longer used, disable it.

                HighPW-004Tier Zero account logged on to computers outside Tier Zero4 findings · 8 objects
                How to fix this kind of findingstep-by-step guide

                Category: Attack path Typical owner: AD / identity team together with the admins who own the account

                What this finding means

                A Tier Zero account (for example a Domain Admin) had a session on servers or workstations outside Tier Zero. While logged on, and often afterwards, its credentials are in that computer's memory, so anyone with admin rights on the computer can take them.

                Why attackers care

                Attackers who gain local admin on any listed computer dump LSASS or steal Kerberos tickets (OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory, T1003.001) and immediately become Domain Admin. This is one of the most common paths in real intrusions and pentests, and usually the biggest choke point in the report's Remediation path tab.

                Before you change anything

                • Ask the account owner why they log on to those computers (RDP, scheduled task, service, mapped drive). Event 4624 on the computer shows logon type: 2/10 interactive or RDP, 3 network, 4 batch, 5 service.
                • Services or scheduled tasks running as a Tier Zero account must be moved to a dedicated, non-privileged service account (or gMSA) first, or they will break.
                • Make sure each admin has a separate, non-Tier Zero account for daily work.

                Fix

                Option A: Separate accounts per tier and deny Tier Zero logon elsewhere (recommended)
                1. Give the admin a normal account for workstations and a Tier 1 account for servers if needed.
                2. In Group Policy Management, edit a GPO linked to all non-Tier Zero computers: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment.
                3. Add the Tier Zero groups (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins) to Deny log on locally, Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services, Deny log on as a batch job and Deny log on as a service. Deny access to this computer from the network also stops network sign-ins, but it blocks remote administration of those computers with Tier Zero accounts as well.
                4. Log off the account on the listed computers, or reboot them, to clear cached credentials. If any of them may have been compromised, change the account's password.
                Option B: Authentication Policy Silos
                1. In Active Directory Administrative Center > Authentication, create an authentication policy and silo that allows Tier Zero accounts to authenticate only from Tier Zero computers (requires Windows Server 2012 R2+ domain functional level).
                2. Assign the accounts and Tier Zero computers to the silo; test in audit mode first.
                Option C: Protected Users

                Add the account to Protected Users: no NTLM, no delegation, no cached credentials, 4-hour TGTs. Test first: it breaks NTLM-only apps for that account.

                PowerShell
                Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Where has the account logged on recently? (run on a computer from the finding)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName = 'Security'; Id = 4624 } -MaxEvents 2000 |
    Where-Object { $_.Properties[5].Value -eq '<Account>' } |
    Select-Object TimeCreated, @{ n = 'LogonType'; e = { $_.Properties[8].Value } }

# Services and scheduled tasks running as the account on a computer
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -ComputerName <Computer> | Where-Object StartName -like '*<Account>*'
Get-ScheduledTask -CimSession <Computer> | Where-Object { $_.Principal.UserId -like '*<Account>*' }

# Add the account to Protected Users (after testing)
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Protected Users" -Members "<Account>"

                Verify

                After the deny rights apply (gpupdate /force, or the next refresh), a logon attempt by the Tier Zero account on a listed computer must fail. Collect again (or use Retest on the finding) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

                Rollback

                Remove the groups from the Deny user rights in the GPO (or unlink it) and run gpupdate /force; remove the account from Protected Users with Remove-ADGroupMember "Protected Users" -Members "<Account>".

                References

                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/credentials-protection-and-management/protected-users-security-group
                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/credentials-protection-and-management/authentication-policies-and-authentication-policy-silos

                HighPW-002Account or group outside Tier Zero can DCSync1 finding · 2 objects
                How to fix this kind of findingstep-by-step guide

                Category: Attack path Typical owner: AD / identity team

                What this finding means

                A user, computer or group outside Tier Zero holds both directory replication rights on the domain object: "Replicating Directory Changes" and "Replicating Directory Changes All" (directly or through group membership). Together they let it ask a domain controller for the password hash of any account.

                Why attackers care

                DCSync (OS Credential Dumping: DCSync, T1003.006) lets an attacker who controls this account or group pull the krbtgt hash and every admin hash remotely, without touching a domain controller's disk. With the krbtgt hash they can forge golden tickets and keep domain access until krbtgt is rotated twice. Tools such as Mimikatz and Impacket secretsdump do this in one command.

                Before you change anything

                • Identify what the account or group is. Legitimate holders besides domain controllers are rare: Entra Connect (MSOL_ / AAD sync) accounts, some identity governance, backup or password-sync products.
                • Check whether it actually replicates: on domain controllers, audit "Directory Service Access" and look for event 4662 with the replication GUIDs 1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 and 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 and the account as subject.
                • If it is a sync account that must keep the rights, do not remove them: treat the account and its server as Tier Zero instead (Option B).

                Fix

                Option A: Remove the replication rights (recommended when not needed)
                1. In Active Directory Users and Computers, enable View > Advanced Features.
                2. Right-click the domain, Properties > Security > Advanced.
                3. Find entries for the account (or the group that grants it) with "Replicating Directory Changes" / "Replicating Directory Changes All".
                4. Select each and click Remove, then OK.
                5. If the right comes through a group, remove the account from that group instead.
                Option B: Keep the rights, manage the account as Tier Zero
                1. Add the account and the server it runs on under Additional Tier Zero in Settings.
                2. Restrict logon to that server to Tier Zero admins, protect the account (long random password or gMSA where the product supports it), and monitor event 4662 for replication from any other source.
                3. If the sync server has been retired, disable the account and remove the rights as in Option A.

                By default only Domain Controllers, Enterprise Domain Controllers and Administrators hold both rights on the domain object.

                PowerShell
                Import-Module ActiveDirectory
$domainDN = (Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName
$acl = Get-Acl -Path "AD:\$domainDN"

# Replication extended rights
$getChanges    = [Guid]"1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2"
$getChangesAll = [Guid]"1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2"

# Show who holds them
$acl.Access | Where-Object { $_.ObjectType -in $getChanges, $getChangesAll } |
    Select-Object IdentityReference, ObjectType, IsInherited

# Save the current descriptor, then remove the account's entries
$acl.Sddl | Out-File ".\domain-acl-backup.txt"
$acl.Access | Where-Object {
    $_.ObjectType -in $getChanges, $getChangesAll -and $_.IdentityReference -like "*<Account>"
} | ForEach-Object { [void]$acl.RemoveAccessRule($_) }
Set-Acl -Path "AD:\$domainDN" -AclObject $acl

                Verify

                Re-run the "Show who holds them" query; only domain controllers, Enterprise Domain Controllers, Administrators and intended sync accounts should remain. Collect again (or use Retest on the finding) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

                Rollback

                Restore the saved descriptor: $acl = Get-Acl "AD:\$domainDN"; $acl.SetSecurityDescriptorSddlForm((Get-Content .\domain-acl-backup.txt)); Set-Acl "AD:\$domainDN" $acl

                References

                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/006/
                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-configure-ad-ds-connector-account
                • https://bloodhound.specterops.io/

                MediumPW-008Tier Zero accounts without delegation protection1 finding · 41 users
                How to fix this kind of findingstep-by-step guide

                Category: Hygiene Typical owner: AD / identity team

                What this finding means

                These Tier Zero user accounts are neither members of the Protected Users group nor marked "Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated". Their credentials can therefore be cached on the computers they log on to, and their Kerberos tickets can be forwarded by any service trusted for delegation.

                Why attackers care

                An attacker who controls a server trusted for unconstrained or constrained delegation can impersonate any delegatable account that authenticates to it, including Domain Admins (Kerberos delegation abuse, MITRE ATT&CK T1558). Accounts outside Protected Users also leave NTLM hashes and long-lived credentials in LSASS memory, which tools like Mimikatz extract (OS Credential Dumping, T1003.001). Protected Users removes both of these options for its members.

                Before you change anything

                • Protected Users members cannot use NTLM, DES or RC4 Kerberos encryption, Kerberos delegation, or cached (offline) logons, and their Kerberos TGTs last 4 hours. Anything that relies on these will break for the account.
                • Never add service accounts or computer accounts to Protected Users. Use the "sensitive and cannot be delegated" flag (Option B) for service accounts that are Tier Zero.
                • Check for NTLM use by the account first: enable NTLM auditing ("Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain") and review event 8004 on domain controllers, or 4624 events with Authentication Package NTLM.
                • Make sure the domain functional level is Windows Server 2012 R2 or later. Protected Users only takes full effect from that level.
                • Keep at least one break-glass account outside Protected Users in case Kerberos fails. Store its password offline.

                Fix

                Option A: Add Tier Zero user accounts to Protected Users (recommended)
                1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc).
                2. Go to the Users container and open the Protected Users group.
                3. Members tab > Add. Add one test admin account first.
                4. Sign out and sign back in with that account. Confirm your admin tools still work.
                5. Add the remaining interactive Tier Zero admin accounts listed in the finding.
                Option B: Mark the account "sensitive and cannot be delegated"

                Use this for accounts that cannot join Protected Users, such as Tier Zero service accounts.

                1. In dsa.msc, open the account > Account tab.
                2. Under Account options, tick Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated.
                3. Click OK.
                PowerShell
                Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Option A: add an interactive admin account to Protected Users
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Protected Users" -Members "<Account>"

# Option B: block delegation for an account that cannot join Protected Users
Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -AccountNotDelegated $true

                Verify

                # Members of Protected Users
Get-ADGroupMember -Identity "Protected Users" | Select-Object SamAccountName

# Accounts flagged as not delegatable
Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties AccountNotDelegated |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, AccountNotDelegated

                Collect again (or use Retest on the finding) and confirm the finding ID is gone (or lists fewer accounts).

                Rollback

                • Remove the account from the group: Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity "Protected Users" -Members "<Account>". The change applies at the account's next logon. Existing tickets expire within 4 hours.
                • Clear the flag: Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -AccountNotDelegated $false.

                References

                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/credentials-protection-and-management/protected-users-security-group
                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/
                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/

                MediumPW-009Stale Tier Zero accounts1 finding · 2 users
                How to fix this kind of findingstep-by-step guide

                Category: Hygiene Typical owner: AD / identity team

                What this finding means

                These accounts are enabled and hold Tier Zero privileges, but they have not logged on within the configured period (90 days by default) or have never logged on at all. Nobody appears to use them, yet they could still take over the domain.

                Why attackers care

                Dormant privileged accounts are ideal targets. Their passwords are often old or reused, and nobody notices when they are used again. An attacker who guesses, sprays or cracks such a password gets Tier Zero access through a legitimate account (Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts, MITRE ATT&CK T1078.002). Unused accounts also tend to sit outside monitoring and MFA rollouts.

                Before you change anything

                • Confirm with the account owner (from the description, the manager attribute or your IAM system) that the account is not needed.
                • Service accounts may authenticate without updating lastLogonTimestamp the way you expect. Check for recent 4624 / 4768 / 4769 events for the account on domain controllers before disabling.
                • lastLogonTimestamp replicates with up to a 14-day lag. Treat dates as approximate.
                • For break-glass accounts that are meant to be unused, document them and accept the finding as a risk in Settings, with a review date, instead of disabling them.

                Fix

                Option A: Disable the account (recommended)
                1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc).
                2. Find the account, right-click > Disable Account.
                3. Add a note in the Description field (date, ticket number) and leave it disabled for a grace period (for example 30 days) before deleting it.
                Option B: Remove the privileged group memberships

                If the account must stay enabled, for example for a rarely used process:

                1. Open the account > Member Of tab.
                2. Remove Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Administrators and any other Tier Zero group.
                3. Grant only the specific rights the process needs.
                PowerShell
                Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Review last logon and group memberships first
Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties LastLogonDate, MemberOf, Description |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, LastLogonDate, Description, MemberOf

# Option A: disable and annotate
Disable-ADAccount -Identity "<Account>"
Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Description "Disabled <date> - stale Tier Zero account, ticket <ID>"

# Option B: remove from a privileged group instead
Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Members "<Account>" -Confirm:$false

                Verify

                Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties Enabled, MemberOf |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, Enabled, MemberOf

                Collect again (or use Retest on the finding) and confirm the finding ID is gone (or lists fewer accounts).

                Rollback

                • Re-enable the account with Enable-ADAccount -Identity "<Account>".
                • Re-add removed group memberships with Add-ADGroupMember. Record the original memberships (the review command above) before removing them.

                References

                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/002/
                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/plan/security-best-practices/implementing-least-privilege-administrative-models

                MediumPW-010Old Tier Zero passwords1 finding · 25 users
                How to fix this kind of findingstep-by-step guide

                Category: Hygiene Typical owner: AD / identity team (service account owners for service accounts)

                What this finding means

                These Tier Zero accounts have passwords older than the configured limit (365 days by default). The longer a privileged password lives, the more places it may have leaked to: old backups, scripts, memory dumps, password managers of former staff, or earlier breaches.

                Why attackers care

                Attackers routinely recover old credential material, such as NTDS.dit backups, LSASS dumps from decommissioned servers and cracked hashes from earlier intrusions. A password that has not changed since then still works (Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts, MITRE ATT&CK T1078.002). If an attacker has the NTLM hash of an unchanged account, pass-the-hash keeps working until the password changes (Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash, T1550.002).

                Before you change anything

                • For service accounts, find every place the password is configured (services, scheduled tasks, IIS application pools, application config files, scripts) before rotating. Check 4625 failures on domain controllers right after the change to catch anything you missed.
                • Check for "password never expires": Get-ADUser <Account> -Properties PasswordNeverExpires.
                • Interactive admins should change their own password so they choose and store it securely.
                • Prefer migrating service accounts to group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA), which rotate automatically.

                Fix

                Option A: Rotate the password now (recommended)
                1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc).
                2. Right-click the account > Reset Password.
                3. Set a long random password (25+ characters for service accounts) and store it in your privileged access vault.
                4. For service accounts, update every place that uses the password, then restart the dependent services.
                Option B: Move service accounts to a gMSA
                1. Create a gMSA (New-ADServiceAccount) that the computers running the service are allowed to use.
                2. Install it on those computers (Install-ADServiceAccount) and reconfigure the service to run as <Domain>\<gMSA>$ with an empty password.
                3. Disable the old account once the service runs under the gMSA.
                PowerShell
                Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Review password age
Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties PasswordLastSet, PasswordNeverExpires |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, PasswordLastSet, PasswordNeverExpires

# Reset the password (prompts for the new value without echoing it)
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity "<Account>" -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString "New password")

# Optional: let the normal password policy apply again
Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -PasswordNeverExpires $false

                Verify

                Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties PasswordLastSet |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, PasswordLastSet

                Collect again (or use Retest on the finding) and confirm the finding ID is gone (or lists fewer accounts).

                Rollback

                A password cannot be "un-rotated". If a service breaks, set the new password wherever the service is configured (or reset again to a value you control and update the service), then restart the service. Check 4625 events to find the failing computer.

                References

                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/002/
                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/
                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/group-managed-service-accounts/group-managed-service-accounts-overview

                Step-by-step guide for PW-010

                MediumPW-011Computers without LAPS1 finding · 538 computers
                How to fix this kind of findingstep-by-step guide

                Category: Hygiene Typical owner: Desktop / server team, with the AD team for schema and permissions

                What this finding means

                These enabled computers (domain controllers excluded) do not have their local administrator password managed by LAPS. Their built-in local Administrator password is probably set by an image or a script, and is often identical across many computers.

                Standalone managed service accounts (sMSA) are not reported: they appear as computer-like objects but have no interactive local administrator, so LAPS doesn't apply. Pathwarden recognizes them from SharpHound's msa flag, and in RustHound-CE or built-in collections (which type an sMSA as a computer with no flag) from its membership of the domain's Managed Service Accounts container.

                Why attackers care

                After compromising one computer, an attacker dumps the local Administrator hash from the SAM and tries it everywhere. If the password is shared, every computer with the same password falls (Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash, MITRE ATT&CK T1550.002, and Lateral Movement via SMB/Windows Admin Shares, T1021.002). This is one of the most common ways a single phished workstation turns into domain-wide compromise during a pentest.

                Before you change anything

                • Windows LAPS is built into Windows 10/11 and Windows Server 2019 and later with the April 2023 update. Older systems need legacy Microsoft LAPS, or an upgrade.
                • Decide who may read passwords. By default only Domain Admins can. Grant read access to a dedicated helpdesk/desktop group per OU, never to broad groups.
                • Check for tooling that relies on the shared local admin password (deployment scripts, remote support tools) and move it to LAPS retrieval or domain accounts first.
                • The schema update is forest-wide and needs Schema Admins rights. Plan it with the AD team.

                Fix

                Option A: Deploy Windows LAPS by Group Policy (recommended)
                1. Extend the schema once: run Update-LapsADSchema as a Schema Admin.
                2. Let computers write their own password: Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission -Identity "<OU>".
                3. Grant read access to the support group: Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission -Identity "<OU>" -AllowedPrincipals "<Domain>\<SupportGroup>".
                4. In Group Policy Management, create a GPO linked to the OU and open Computer Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > System > LAPS.
                5. Enable Configure password backup directory = Active Directory, and set Password Settings (complexity, length 15+, age 30 days).
                6. Run gpupdate /force on a test computer and check that a password appears (see Verify).
                7. Widen the GPO to the remaining OUs in the finding.
                Option B: Intune (for Entra-joined or co-managed devices)

                Use an Intune Endpoint security > Account protection > Local admin password solution policy with the backup directory set to Active Directory (for hybrid-joined) or Entra ID.

                PowerShell
                # One-time forest preparation (Schema Admins)
Update-LapsADSchema

# Per OU: allow computers to update their own password attributes
Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission -Identity "<OU>"

# Per OU: allow the support group to read passwords
Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission -Identity "<OU>" -AllowedPrincipals "<Domain>\<SupportGroup>"

# After GPO deployment: confirm a computer has a managed password
Get-LapsADPassword -Identity "<Computer>" -AsPlainText

                Verify

                Get-LapsADPassword -Identity "<Computer>" returns a password and an expiration time. On the client, the event log Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > LAPS > Operational shows successful password updates. Collect again (or use Retest on the finding) and confirm the finding ID is gone (or lists fewer computers).

                Rollback

                Unlink or disable the LAPS GPO. Computers keep their last LAPS-set password, so retrieve it with Get-LapsADPassword before removing read permissions. The schema extension is permanent but harmless.

                References

                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/laps/laps-overview
                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/laps/laps-scenarios-windows-server-active-directory
                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/

                How to fix it

                Deploy Windows LAPS to these computers, and allow only the admins of each tier to read the stored passwords. Computers that can't run Windows LAPS, such as Linux computers and appliances, need another way to get a unique local password. Delete computer objects that no longer exist.

                Step-by-step guide for PW-011 · https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/laps/laps-overview

                LowPW-022Account or group outside a Privilege Zone controls a zone object44 findings · 88 objects
                How to fix this kind of findingstep-by-step guide

                Category: Attack path Typical owner: Owner of the Privilege Zone (for example the server team for "Tier 1 servers"), with the AD team for permissions

                What this finding means

                An account or group that is neither in the named Privilege Zone nor in Tier Zero has a right over an object inside the zone. That could be an AD permission (GenericAll, WriteDacl, WriteOwner, ForceChangePassword, AddMember, ...), local administrator or remote access rights on a zone computer, delegation rights, or a GPO link. Whoever controls that account or group can take over the zone object, so the zone boundary your tiering model assumes does not hold.

                Why attackers care

                Attackers rarely go for the target directly. They compromise whatever is easiest (a helpdesk account, an old service account, a workstation) and follow permissions from there. A single leftover delegation, for example a support group with local admin rights on a sensitive server, turns any compromise of that support group into a compromise of the zone (Account Manipulation, MITRE ATT&CK T1098, and Remote Services, T1021). The finding's exposure figure shows how many users and computers can reach the controlling account or group.

                Before you change anything

                • Decide whether the account or group should administer the zone. If it should, the right answer is to add it to the zone on the Privilege Zones page (and protect it like the zone). Do not remove the permission.
                • Find what uses the right: for local admin rights, check 4624 logon events (type 3/10) on the computer. For AD permissions, check the account's role with its owner.
                • If the finding says the permission is inherited, change it on the parent OU or container. That change affects every object below it, so review those objects too.

                Fix

                Option A: Remove the right (recommended)

                The finding's "fix" line names the relationship. Common cases:

                1. AD permission (ACE): In Active Directory Users and Computers, enable View > Advanced Features, open the object (or the parent OU for inherited ACEs) > Security > Advanced, select the entry for the account or group and click Remove.
                2. Local Administrators / Remote Desktop Users: remove the account or group from the local group on the computer, or from the GPO / Intune policy that adds it (Computer Configuration > Preferences > Control Panel Settings > Local Users and Groups, or Restricted Groups).
                3. Group membership (AddMember on a zone group): remove the permission from the group's Security tab as in step 1.
                4. GPO link / GPO edit rights: restrict who can edit the linked GPO (Group Policy Management > GPO > Delegation), or unlink it from the zone OU.
                Option B: Bring the account or group into the zone

                If the account or group legitimately manages the zone, add it to the zone on the Privilege Zones page. Then manage it with the same controls as the zone: no use from lower-tier computers, and admin accounts dedicated to this tier.

                PowerShell
                Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Show ACEs for the account or group on a zone object
$dn = (Get-ADObject -Filter "Name -eq '<Object>'").DistinguishedName
(Get-Acl "AD:$dn").Access | Where-Object { $_.IdentityReference -like "*<Account>*" } |
    Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights, IsInherited

# Remove those ACEs (explicit ones only; fix inherited ones on the parent)
$acl = Get-Acl "AD:$dn"
$acl.Access | Where-Object { $_.IdentityReference -like "*<Account>*" -and -not $_.IsInherited } |
    ForEach-Object { [void]$acl.RemoveAccessRule($_) }
Set-Acl -Path "AD:$dn" -AclObject $acl

# Local admin rights on a zone computer (run on that computer)
Remove-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "<Domain>\<Account>"

                Verify

                Re-run the Get-Acl command above, or Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" on the computer, and confirm the account or group is gone. Collect again (or use Retest on the finding) and confirm the finding ID is gone. The zone's row in the report shows the accounts that still have an attack path to the zone.

                Rollback

                Before removing an ACE, export it: (Get-Acl "AD:$dn").Sddl | Out-File acl-backup.txt. Restore it with $acl.SetSecurityDescriptorSddlForm((Get-Content acl-backup.txt)) followed by Set-Acl. Re-add local group members with Add-LocalGroupMember.

                References

                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/
                • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/
                • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/privileged-access-workstations/privileged-access-access-model

                Finding ID
                PW-022-4e17fe2b0f1749dd

                Not closed by the remediation path. Fix it directly: see How to fix it.

                Why it matters

                R01-HELPDESK@SCALE.LOCAL is outside the R01 servers zone but has ForceChangePassword on the user R01S00-U00089@SCALE.LOCAL, which belongs to it. Whoever controls R01-HELPDESK@SCALE.LOCAL controls R01S00-U00089@SCALE.LOCAL, so the zone boundary doesn't hold. Deny entries: not checked. Pathwarden reads allowed permissions only.

                How to fix it

                Remove the Active Directory security permission ForceChangePassword that R01-HELPDESK@SCALE.LOCAL holds on the user R01S00-U00089@SCALE.LOCAL. If R01-HELPDESK@SCALE.LOCAL needs to change R01S00-U00089@SCALE.LOCAL, delegate only the rights it needs. It is inherited from R01S00-USERS@SCALE.LOCAL or a container above it: fix the entry there, where it is defined, and check inheritance on the objects below it, because the change applies to all of them. Leave the right to change the user only with the zone's administrators. If R01-HELPDESK@SCALE.LOCAL administers this zone, add it to the zone instead.
